{{Short description|Concept in critical data studies}}
'''Data imaginaries''' are a form of cultural [[Imaginary (sociology)|imaginary]] related to social conceptions of [[data]], a concept that comes from the field of [[critical data studies]]. A data imaginary is a particular [[Framing (social sciences)|framing]] of data that defines what data are and what can be done with them.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Kitchin |first=Rob |title=The Data Revolution: A Critical Analysis of Big Data, Open Data & Data Infrastructures |publisher=SAGE Publications |year=2022 |isbn=978-1-5297-3375-4 |edition=2nd |location=Los Angeles, CA |pages=29 |language=en |oclc=1285687714}}</ref> Imaginaries are produced by social institutions and practices and they influence how people understand and use the object of the imaginary, in this case data.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last1=Bottici |first1=Chiara |title=The Politics of Imagination |last2=Challand |first2=Benoît |publisher=Birkbeck Law Press |year=2011 |isbn=978-0-415-60154-2 |location=Abingdon, Oxon |pages=1–15 |language=en |oclc=641536004}}</ref>

Different data imaginaries compete to be considered [[common sense]]. The current most established data imaginary is that of [[Analytics|data analytics]], which treats data as a neutral resource from which people can extract value.<ref name=":7">{{Cite book |last=Kitchin |first=Rob |title=The Data Revolution: A Critical Analysis of Big Data, Open Data & Data Infrastructures |date=2022 |publisher=SAGE Publications |isbn=978-1-5297-3375-4 |edition=2nd |location=Los Angeles, CA |pages=145–146 |language=en |oclc=1285687714}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Gray |first=Jonathan |date=2018 |title=Three Aspects of Data Worlds |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/2291630136 |journal=Krisis |volume=38 |language=English |issue=1 |pages=4–17|doi=10.21827/krisis.38.1.38827 |id={{ProQuest|2291630136}} |doi-access=free }}</ref> Competing imaginaries include those of data activists, prioritizing data justice, and critical data studies, prioritizing consideration of the context around data.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Baack |first=Stefan |date=2018 |title=Civic Tech at mySociety: How the Imagined Affordances of Data Shape Data Activism |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/2291068799 |journal=Krisis |language=English |issue=1 |pages=53|id={{ProQuest|2291068799}} }}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last=Kitchin |first=Rob |title=The Data Revolution: A Critical Analysis of Big Data, Open Data & Data Infrastructures |publisher=SAGE Publications |year=2022 |isbn=978-1-5297-3375-4 |edition=2nd |location=Los Angeles, CA |pages=117–118 |language=en |oclc=1285687714}}</ref>

== Theoretical basis ==
A data imaginary is a particular framing of data, according to [[Rob Kitchin|Kitchin]] consisting of "how [data] are understood and normatively conceived of within a population or by stakeholders."<ref name=":0" /> It is a [[Social constructivism|social constructivist]] theoretical concept that comes from the field of critical data studies, which is concerned with identifying these frames and questioning them rather than just taking them at face value.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kitchin |first=Rob |title=The Data Revolution: A Critical Analysis of Big Data, Open Data & Data Infrastructures |publisher=SAGE Publications |year=2022 |isbn=978-1-5297-3375-4 |edition=2nd |location=Los Angeles, CA |pages=21 |language=en |oclc=1285687714}}</ref> According to Baack, this context is important to consider, as "what data [afford] to whom does not only depend on the technological properties of data, but is fundamentally social, and both culturally and historically situated."<ref name=":3" /> Examining data imaginaries treats the narratives around data as separate from the data themselves, focusing on the former.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dourish |first1=Paul |last2=Gómez Cruz |first2=Edgar |date=2018 |title=Datafication and data fiction: Narrating data and narrating with data |journal=Big Data & Society |language=en |volume=5 |issue=2 |pages=7–8 |doi=10.1177/2053951718784083 |s2cid=149991014 |issn=2053-9517|doi-access=free |hdl=1959.4/unsworks_54920 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

The concept of data imaginaries draws on the sociological imaginary. In sociology, imaginaries are social constructions that stem from social institutions and practices that prioritize different aspects of a social structure, in this case ideas about the use of data.<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal |last=Dencik |first=Lina |date=2018 |title=Surveillance Realism and the Politics of Imagination: Is There No Alternative? |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/2291069053 |journal=Krisis |language=English |issue=1 |pages=32|id={{ProQuest|2291069053}} }}</ref><ref name=":1" /> According to Vanheeswijck, one of the most significant writers on this topic is [[Charles Taylor (philosopher)|Charles Taylor]] in his book [[A Secular Age]], which defines social imaginaries as common understandings that facilitate collective actions and exist in cultural practices rather than being theoretically articulated.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Vanheeswijck |first=Guido M. |date=2017 |title=The Philosophical Genealogy of Taylor's Social Imaginaries: A Complex History of Ideas and Predecessors |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1353/jhi.2017.0026 |journal=Journal of the History of Ideas |volume=78 |issue=3 |pages=473–496 |doi=10.1353/jhi.2017.0026 |pmid=28757490 |s2cid=22688362 |issn=1086-3222|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Taylor |first=Charles |title=A Secular Age |date=2007 |publisher=Harvard University Press |isbn=978-0-674-02676-6 |location=Cambridge, Mass. |oclc=85766076}}</ref> Another contributory work to this field is [[Benedict Anderson]]'s book [[Imagined Communities]], which argues that nationalism is based in "[[imagined community|imagined communities]]" formed around geography and data tools such as censuses.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Anderson |first=Benedict |title=Imagined Communities: Reflections on the Origin and Spread of Nationalism |publisher=Verso |year=2016 |isbn=978-1-78478-675-5 |edition=Revised |location=London |language=en |oclc=932385849}}</ref> This concept is a geographically focused understanding of data imaginaries. Theories of the social imaginary assert that these constructions are not fake or meaningless, as they direct how people think about a concept like data and what they think is able to be done with them.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bucher |first=Taina |date=2017-01-02 |title=The algorithmic imaginary: exploring the ordinary affects of Facebook algorithms |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1369118X.2016.1154086 |journal=Information, Communication & Society |language=en |volume=20 |issue=1 |pages=31 |doi=10.1080/1369118X.2016.1154086 |s2cid=147672955 |issn=1369-118X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> According to Denick, social imaginaries enable social practices by providing ways to understand the world.<ref name=":8" /> Data imaginaries are the narratives that shape how people conceive of and act upon data, though data do not always live up to the ideal aspirations presented.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gray |first=Jonathan |date=2018 |title=Three Aspects of Data Worlds |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/2291630136 |journal=Krisis |language=English |issue=1 |pages=13|id={{ProQuest|2291630136}} }}</ref>

== Competing imaginaries ==
According to Kitchin, "different groups hold varying data imaginaries, concerning what data are generated and how, for what purpose," and how they "can serve particular agendas."<ref name=":0" /> People with differing opinions on how data ''should'' be used may share the same imaginary, which is concerned instead with how data ''can'' be used.<ref name=":0" /> People with alternative data imaginaries can challenge and reinterpret dominant ideas to promote their own understandings.<ref name=":5">{{Cite book |last=Kitchin |first=Rob |title=The Data Revolution: A Critical Analysis of Big Data, Open Data & Data Infrastructures |publisher=SAGE Publications |year=2022 |isbn=978-1-5297-3375-4 |edition=2nd |location=Los Angeles, CA |pages=30 |language=en |oclc=1285687714}}</ref> Since this is a competition of ideas, a particular imaginary is 'successful' when people, the more the better, consider that imaginary common sense, i.e. the obvious way the world works.<ref name=":0" />

=== Data analytics ===
[[File:Data-driven vs data-brokering.png|thumb|Companies that harness data to increase profits and members of the data broker industry share a data analytics data imaginary, though they have different business practices.]]
The data analytics imaginary is the most established one in modern western society.<ref name=":7" /> Kitchin has defined it as framing data as "speedy (rapid insights), accessible (easily interpreted), revealing (extracting hidden knowledge), panoramic (all-seeing), prophetic (able to foresee and shape the future), and smart (possessing latent intelligence)."<ref name=":0" /> This imaginary treats data as a single social or economic resource akin to a product like oil, requiring an equivalent supporting infrastructure.<ref name=":2" /> Data are considering a mine-able resource from which value can be extracted.<ref name=":2" />

An example of the influence of this framing, according to Cinnamon, is how data are considered the primary solution for urban challenges.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last=Cinnamon |first=Jonathan |date=2019 |title=Visual Data Justice? Datafication of Urban Informality in South Africa Using 360° Imaging Technologies |url=https://www.ssrn.com/abstract=3456196 |journal=SSRN Electronic Journal |language=en |pages=5 |doi=10.2139/ssrn.3456196 |s2cid=219341067 |issn=1556-5068|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Furthermore, [[grassroots]] civic activism involving data often embraces this imaginary, challenging particular uses of data but not the notions of how they can be used.<ref name=":6" />

=== Data activists ===
Data activists have competing imaginaries to the more common data analytics imaginary. These can vary depending on individual priorities, as they are not as well established, but they tend to prioritize data justice and community-oriented politics.<ref name=":5" /> These imaginaries challenge current assumptions around [[datafication]] in the modern world.<ref name=":3" />

An example of this framing being used, according to Segura and Waisbord, is activist efforts to oppose social and institutional issues such as gender-based violence and police violence in Latin America by documenting the problems and using the data gathered to advocate for solutions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Segura |first1=María Soledad |last2=Waisbord |first2=Silvio |date=May 2019 |title=Between Data Capitalism and Data Citizenship |url=http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1527476419834519 |journal=Television & New Media |language=en |volume=20 |issue=4 |pages=412–419 |doi=10.1177/1527476419834519 |hdl=11336/112331 |s2cid=150818865 |issn=1527-4764|hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Under this perspective, data are treated as tools to achieve some form of justice rather than as a neutral resource.

=== Critical data studies ===
Critical data studies, the academic discipline that produced the notion of data imaginaries, has its own imaginary.<ref name=":5" /> This imaginary is particularly concerned with the role of power and politics, seeing data as situated within "a complex [[Assemblage (philosophy)|assemblage]] that actively shapes their constitution" according to Rob Kitchin, a leading scholar in the field.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kitchin |first=Rob |title=The Data Revolution: A Critical Analysis of Big Data, Open Data & Data Infrastructures |publisher=SAGE Publications |year=2022 |isbn=978-1-5297-3375-4 |edition=2nd |location=Los Angeles, CA |pages=22 |language=en |oclc=1285687714}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Kitchin |first=Rob |title=The Data Revolution: A Critical Analysis of Big Data, Open Data & Data Infrastructures |publisher=SAGE Publications |year=2022 |isbn=978-1-5297-3375-4 |edition=2nd |location=Los Angeles, CA |pages=117 |language=en |oclc=1285687714}}</ref> Critical data studies challenges the assumption that data are inherently neutral, calling out the framing processes that arise in the methodologies and epistemologies that are applied to data.<ref name=":4" />
